articles.title: Guns going off
articles.content: SHE was articulate, she was poised and she was intelligent. NowRabia Ahsan, television news anchor, entrepreneur and mother to two, is dead. According to news reports, this is how the tragic events unfolded. On the afternoon of November 8, 2026, Rabia Ahsan was at her home in Rawalpindi, incidentally located not far from where Hina Javed, the last woman whose murder I wrote about in this column also died. At around 2.30 pm, Rabia’s mother and sister, who were in the lawn, heard a gunshot. They rushed into the bedroom she shared with her husband. Her sister found Rabia on the ground in a pool of blood and her husband Ahsan Tahir allegedly standing nearby holding a pistol. Police arrested her husband and recovered the weapon. According to City Police Officer Hassan Sukhera, a male domestic worker told the police that Ahsan Tahir had claimed the gun went off accidentally. An FIR, registered on the complaint of her brother Khurram Ahmed, stated among other things that the husband could not produce a licence for the firearm. On Nov 9, the court granted police one-day physical remand of the suspect. The following day, his remand was extended by four days. Investigators sought forensic examinations and a polygraph test, alleging inconsistencies in the husband’s statements to the police. The findings of the test are not yet known. Why do our guns, like our society, hate women so much? According to police sources, the post-mortem examination of Rabia Ahsan’s body did not find any evidence of violence on her body. They said that the spent shell casing and pistol had been sent for forensic examination. The police alleged that the forensic examination and the polygraph would provide further clues as to what transpired in the bedroom that day while the couple were allegedly retrieving winter clothes from their cupboards. In the meantime, her brother Khurram has publicly stated that he believed her husband’s account and did not think this was a deliberate killing. Other family members have also said the relationship was stable and there was no marital tension. There is, however, one important person from Rabia Ahsan’s life who does not agree with the account being presented by the family. Senior journalist Aamir Mateen, Rabia Ahsan’s former co-host alleged in his programme that he personally knew that Ahsan was a victim of domestic violence. He claimed that there were numerous times when he knew that she was going through a very difficult time and was facing tensions at home. At one point, Mateen alleged, Ahsan had left her marital home and was living at the house of a friend for at least a month. Her family then intervened and persuaded her to return home for the sake of the children. Mateen said that he had given a statement to the police and would provide further statements to authorities. Rabia Ahsan’s case remains under investigation. According to police officials, FIRs once registered cannot be withdrawn and the judge in the case will now determine how the case will proceed. It is important, however, to consider the number of times in recent history that wives are found dead and husbands allege that the “gun went off accidentally.” In November 2022, a young wife named Saba who lived in a rented home near Eidgah Ground in Karachi was similarly found dead. Her husband, a police constable, claimed that the gun went off by accident and the bullet happened to strike his wife. His in-laws disputed his claim and registered an FIR. The current status of the case is unclear. In October 2025, a woman namedFarzanawho lived in Gulistan-i-Jauhar was killed in a shooting involving her husband. According to the police, the two had been filming a TikTok video and Farzana asked her husband if the gun was loaded. The husband told her it was not loaded and so she told him to hold the gun at her temple and pulled the trigger. The husband, Ghulam Mustafa, claimed that he had no idea that there was a bullet in the chamber. The husband was arrested but it is unclear whether he has been charged with the crime. Guns in the hands of husbands, it appears, just seem to go off and bullets just happen to miraculously hit their wives. Accidentally firing guns in the hands of husbands seem exceptionally well suited to avoid walls or floors or ceilings that make up a far larger surface area of the surroundings of any given situation and go for the only other human present. Also interestingly, these guns that go off when a man and a woman are present never seem to hit the man — it is always the woman. As we mourn yet another accomplished, intelligent dead woman in Pakistan, one must consider why our guns, like our society, hate women so much? The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: China’s modernisation models
articles.content: PAKISTAN was the first Muslim country to recognise the People’s Republic of China (PRC), with the two countries establishing diplomatic ties on May 21, 1951. During the past 75 years, the relationship has blossomed into an “all-weather strategic cooperative partnership.” During the 1950s and 1960s, despite being a member of Western security alliances, Pakistan helped Beijing break out of its international isolation. Islamabad’s diplomatic mediation in the early 1970s helped in the historic rapprochement between China and the United States. Reciprocally, China has supported Pakistan economically, militarily, and diplomatically, providing unwavering support for its national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and socioeconomic stability. The PRC was established as a single-party ideological state in the Marxist-Leninist tradition. Under the British legacy, Pakistan established a federal state and Westminster-style parliamentary democracy. These governance structures have led to divergence in the modernisation trajectories of the two countries, despite the adoption of similar reform policies. Both China and Pakistan have attempted to resolve the issue of inequitable distribution of agricultural land. The Communist Party of China (CPC) solved the problem by distributing land titles to 300 million peasants using radical measures. Despite possessing less than 10 per cent of the world’s arable land, China produces about 25pc of global grain output. In Pakistan, landlords undermined all attempts at land reforms by falsifying records. Currently, 67pc rural households in Pakistan own no land. Despite having the world’s largest contiguous canal system, Pakistan is ranked 106 out of 123 countries in the Global Hunger Index. The ideal of women’s emancipation has been pursued by both China and Pakistan. Starting with the Marriage Law of 1950, China has passed nearly 100 laws and regulations, including the landmark Law on the Protection of Rights and Interests of Women 1992. Today China, at 65pc, is ahead of the global average in female labour force participation. Traditionally, family life in Pakistan has been ruled by feudal and tribal customs, colonial-era personal laws, and religious precepts. Pakistan promulgated the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 but conditions in rural areas remained unchanged. In the Global Gender Gap Index of the World Economic Forum, Pakistan ranks at the very bottom: 148 out of 148 countries. In China, modernisation emerged as one of the central purposes of the state. Soviet-style five-year plans have been used by both China and Pakistan. Since 1953, China has successfully completed 15 five-year plans. In the process it has been transformed from a subsistence agricultural economy into the largest manufacturing power, the biggest exporter, and the only country in history to achieve a trade surplus of one trillion dollars. Pakistan has implemented eight five-year plans but only the second plan (1960-65) succeeded in achieving its targets. Pakistan discontinued the practice in 1998. Slow growth in the last two decades has pushed Pakistan below its South Asian neighbours in per capita GDP. The country runs an annual trade deficit of around $30 billion and Pakistan has received more assistance packages from the International Monetary Fund than any other country. Similar modernisation measures producing dissimilar outcomes is the result of differences in political ideology, structure of the state, and form of government of China and Pakistan. From the British, Pakistan inherited the tradition of liberalism where the state exists primarily to protect individual rights and private property. It is not an instrument to achieve national goals. Socialism distinguishes between different modes of production and the state is an agent of progress. In China, modernisation emerged as one of the central purposes of the state and the supreme responsibility of the party. Political debates in Pakistan remain confined to changes of government. In Pakistan, modernisation never became the topic of political debate and state resources have never been marshalled to achieve it. In China, the CPC solved the problem of lack of state institutions by building party network. Fusion of the party and the state meant that the party’s directives and policies were seamlessly translated into state legislation and administrative action. The party-state model has proved to be the perfect strategy for building modern bureaucracy. Pakistan inherited the colonial-era civil service but nepotism and patronage gradually eroded its essence of impersonality, specialisation, and merit. With every political government the capacity of the state declined, rendering it incapable of maintaining security, collecting taxes, and enforcing policies. Pakistan adopted multiparty adult franchise democracy but the society had no tradition of resolution of differences through rational discourse, no common civic public good, and no equality. Inevitably, Pakistan’s democracy morphed into demagoguery and populism. The communists enshrined in the Chinese constitution the CPC’s leadership as a foundational pillar of the Chinese state. This allows the ruling party to focus on governance. While Pakistan’s political institutions have pushed the country ever deeper into crises, the combination of progressive ideology, appropriate state model, and correct governance system has allowed China to focus on the grand project of national rejuvenation. For developing countries, the universal lesson is that modernisation is not possible without an effective state but not all state types are equal in their capacity. The Westphalian state model and universal-franchise democracy, when adopted by non-Western societies, do not necessarily result in a functional state and a stable government. To be effective, a state and its governance system must align with local conditions and be in harmony with society’s stage of evolution. Without an effective state machinery, even the most elaborate modernisation plans can neither foster sustainable development nor secure a happy and prosperous life for the people. The writer has a background in public administration. He has worked with international financial institutions, including the World Bank.
articles.author: Syed Sardar Ali

articles.title: Pakistan’s polio paradox
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S latest polio case, a seven-month-old boy in Khyber district reported on Nov 6, is the ninth of 2026 and the seventh in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It is another reminder of how elusive eradication has proved. After three decades of campaigns, billions of dollars of international support, a field force of more than 400,000 workers, and the creation of one of the largest polio programmes in the world, the country has still not eliminated a preventable disease. Pakistan has not turned its ability to run campaigns into a system of public health protection that families trust, and that failure, which lies behind much of the refusal, is why the virus survives. The obstacles usually cited are real: insecurity, population movement, and difficult terrain keep teams from some children, while refusals, misinformation, and religious misconceptions keep others from being vaccinated. They do not account for the survival of the virus in communities that vaccination teams reach campaign after campaign and where families still turn the teams away. The reason lies beyond the vaccine, in the relationship between the state, its health institutions, and the communities they serve, and in whether those communities trust them. Political scientist Bo Rothstein has argued that trust in government depends on the quality and impartiality of public institutions: people trust institutions they experience as fair and reliable. Communication alone does not build trust, and a national health priority cannot command it. It grows out of people’s everyday experience of the state. The polio programme mobilises on a scale few public institutions in Pakistan can match. It deploys hundreds of thousands of vaccinators, maps households, monitors coverage, and returns repeatedly for the children who were missed. That capacity has saved many thousands of children from paralysis and remains essential to eradication. Beside that achievement stands the failure: the state’s ability to reach almost every household with polio drops has not become a working system of routine immunisation and basic healthcare. For many families, particularly in underserved parts of the country, the polio team may be one of the few regular points of contact with the state. A vaccinator arrives at the doorstep, sometimes several times a year, to administer polio drops. The same household may have no functioning health facility within reach, no routine childhood vaccines, no maternal care, and no clean drinking water. The state is visible when it wants to vaccinate a child, and often invisible when that child or family needs anything else. Pakistan’s polio programme has acknowledged that communities are using demand-based boycotts as a bargaining chip to draw attention to their problems. The contrast is sharpest in southern KP, where communities have boycotted polio campaigns to press the government on demands that have gone unanswered for years. Misinformation and religious opposition explain few of these boycotts. The British Medical Journal reported in December 2023 that tribal jirgas in southern KP had declared 677 boycotts during the year, with demands that ran from electricity, roads, and livelihoods to refuse collection. Pakistan’s own polio programme acknowledged that communities were using demand-based boycotts as a bargaining chip to draw attention to their problems. When a vaccination round is the only occasion on which citizens can obtain basic services, the fault lies in the system of government as a whole. In some places a boycott is one of the few acts to which the government is compelled to respond, and communities have learnt as much. The frontline has weaknesses of its own. Too few female vaccinators and frequent changes of team members, with thin training for all of them, spoil the encounter at the door. Vaccinators do not always explain convincingly why a child needs repeated doses, least of all to parents who believe that earlier campaigns should have been enough, and programmes make too little use of trusted local figures who understand the concerns of families. Even a better trained and more persuasive team, though, cannot make up for the absence of reliable public services. Repeated visits can also do harm when families experience them as an imposition. For families who see little improvement in their lives, each arrival of a polio team can confirm that the state cares about one disease and one campaign, and little about the wellbeing of their children. The response is to make vaccination part of a broader and more consistent public health presence, by strengthening routine immunisation and primary healthcare. The outreach capacity the polio programme has built should find the children routine immunisation has missed and connect their families with regular health services. That takes trained health workers, reliable vaccine supplies, accessible facilities, and continuity of care, well beyond the occasional catch-up activities attached to polio campaigns, so that immunisation becomes a regular function of the district health system. Behind this is the institutional separation between the polio programme and the wider health system. For years the National and Provincial Emergency Operations Centres have run as a well-funded parallel structure, answerable in large part to international donors, which mobilises large resources for campaign days while the provincial health departments beside them remain short of funds and bound by procedure. The dedicated funding, staffing, surveillance, and management arrangements that let the polio programme operate at scale belong inside the permanent health infrastructure of the provinces. Communities also need channels for their wider concerns, through local administration and elected representatives, and those channels have to work independently of vaccination campaigns. Otherwise the government teaches communities that withholding children from vaccination is an effective way to secure electricity, water, or roads. The responsibility rests with the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, with the provincial governments, above all in KP, and with international donors, who should measure success by the strength of district health services as well as by the number of children reached in each round. Eradication depends on the campaigns, with better trained and more representative teams, and on what the campaigns cannot supply: a health system that protects children between rounds. When a vaccination team arrives at a door, the family should see it as part of a state that also protects their children and listens to them. Until that is so, Pakistan may go on running polio campaigns, and the conditions that make eradication so difficult will stay as they are. The writer is a strategic communication and public health professional, with experience across Asia, Africa and the Middle East.
articles.author: Fayyaz Ahmad Khan

articles.title: Derailed by design
articles.content: PAKISTAN Railways has become synonymous with the image of a decaying organisation: accident-prone, loss-making and inefficient. Not many are willing to admit that mismanagement, unsteady wagons, rickety tracks and 18th-century mindset have reduced the Railways to a near-death existence. Even when it reluctantly continues to chug, rattle and rumble, everyone knows that it is managed and operated in a way not much different from a lorry adda across the road. The only option left seems to lie in the old Dakota Indian tribal wisdom: “When you discover that you are riding a dead horse, the best strategy is to dismount.” Pakistan Railways has simply run out of steam. A meltdown was only natural. Managerially, technically and financially bankrupt, it finds it impossible to transport passengers and goods safely and efficiently. It is headed by a bureaucrat and a politician. While declaring a railway emergency, the only actions the minister in charge could think of were punishments received by schoolchildren. Come to work on Sundays, no leave for three months, send daily reports (homework) to the ministry and use trains for travelling on duty. Even a novice would immediately figure out the pointlessness of these measures. A better informed and competent management would have suggested identifying root causes, taking actions to prevent their recurrence and verifying them for their effectiveness. Imagine a railway in the year 2026 that cannot use even a basic email system for its routine internal and external communication (a disease proudly shared by the entire government of Pakistan.) Reportedly, an experimental email was recently sent to 40 senior officials of the Railways. Thirty-nine never responded, while one was responded to by a clerk saying that a reply was not possible due to the absence of the boss. Pakistan Railways needs non-political & professional management. Compare the sense of responsibility and ethics that differentiate Pakistan Railways from the rest of the world. Following the train derailment at Hatfield, UK on Oct 17, 2000, which killed four passengers, the Railtrack CEO Gerald Corbett took less than 24 hours to tender his resignation. Mohsen Aghaie, the head of the Iranian Railways was quick to resign after a train collision that killed 44 people in Iran in November 2016, describing his departure as a matter of social responsibility and sympathy for the survivors. Pakistan Railways, on the other hand, met with 448 railway disasters between 2021 and 2025, leaving 169 dead and over 400 injured or crippled for life. Not a single Railways chairman even remotely contemplated a resignation. There is no record of any official above grade 19 ever having been held accountable. No wonder the lack of accountability has helped the Railways perfect the art of digging progressively deeper pits and incurring bigger losses each year. It incurred a financial loss of Rs47.49 billion in 2022, Rs48.2bn in 2023, Rs51.38bn in 2024 and Rs61.19bn in 2025. What crime have the people of Pakistan committed to carry such loss-making and life-extracting burden on their shoulders? Track-related derailments, unmanned crossings and train collisions are the three most cited reasons for the repeated railway accidents. Pakistan Railways management has been negligent of not addressing these issues. A quick root cause analysis and effective corrective actions could have fixed these issues for good. Not equipped to either think or act on modern professional lines, it has finally come to an expected dead end. Can a clueless bureaucratic structure that allows human waste to fall directly on railway tracks, from stationary and moving trains, be entrusted to undertake the task of running a Railways system? Pakistan Ra-ilways needs to replace its current setup with a completely non-political, non-bureaucratic and professional management. It needs a world-class occupational health and safety system. It needs a proactive hazard identification and risk assessment programme to fix its fragile tracks, its 1,416 unmanned crossings, and its archaic communication system. For all this, the Railways does not need billions of dollars. It needs billions of neurons. Every developed country’s railway has a system called Occupational Health and Safety Management System based on national or international standards such as ISO 45001. Pakistan Railways appears to have no clue of any such system. Being an occupational health and safety engineer, may I humbly offer to spend two months (as an entirely pro bono activity) to help Pakistan Railways set up such a world-class safety management system. The writer is an industrial engineer and a volunteer social activist.
articles.author: Naeem Sadiq

articles.title: Referendum talk
articles.content: THERE is quite a bit of noise and confusion emanating from Islamabad on the question of new provinces. The defence minister, Khawaja Asif, recently suggested the possibility of there being as many as12 provincesunder a new configuration, drawn on administrative rather than ethnic or linguistic lines. Now, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi wants to hold a referendum to ‘settle’ the matter. In between, there has been talk of a 28th amendment being rushed through before the year is out. Which one is it going to be? Interestingly, Mr Naqvi has alsoclaimedthat he and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari are “almost on the same page”. He was referring to the latter’s suggestion for a “political reset”, but one wonders if there’s more to it. It would be difficult to square an agreement on new provinces, given the PPP’s stated stance so far. Mr Bhutto-Zardari only recently said he’d like to see the matter buried. Is one to understand that while the PPP is opposing any division of Sindh, it is more relaxed to the possibility of new units elsewhere? If so, it would not be standing on principle. It cannot be that the party wants one province’s boundaries to be respected as sacred while every other’s are considered negotiable. Unless the PPP is deliberately using Sindh as a bargaining chip, it should issue a clarification with a clear, consistent position on new administrative units, not one tailored to protect its home turf. As regards the possibility of a referendum, it must be pointed out that while there is no harm in conducting one, it will not clear the constitutional hurdle. Article 239(4) requires any amendment to a province’s limits to be passed by two-thirds of that province’s assembly. No matter how resoundingly a referendum is passed, it will not override that condition. This suggests the idea was not thought through. There is also the question of credibility. The chief election commissioner recently accused the federal government of trying to sabotage Islamabad’s local government polls by creating hurdles in the appointment of teachers for election duties. How can a government that is not even letting the federal capital elect its own councils be preaching about bringing power closer to the people through new administrative units? To be clear, none of the above means that any debate on administrative reforms is illegitimate. However, a change of this magnitude must be built on consensus, not handed down by a dispensation whose mandate remains contested. If the ruling parties want new provinces, or a referendum on them, they should put it in their manifestos and seek a mandate at the next general election. If voters endorse it, the next parliament can act. Until then, the idea is best left to marinate a bit more.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Mineral wealth
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S mineral wealth offers an opportunity to attract investment, earn foreign exchange and support long-term economic growth. But turning this potential into reality will require more than promises. At the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026, Deputy PM Ishaq Dar has promised predictable policies and institutional support to investors interested in the country’s mineral resources. Such assurances are welcome. However, investors will need more than that. The country’s experience with large mining projects has not always inspired confidence. The Reko Diq dispute remains an important reminder of what can happen when agreements and government commitments become contentious. We cannot afford another dispute that damages the country’s credibility. Policy consistency must therefore extend beyond individual governments. That said, mining rights must be awarded through transparent processes, with clear contractual obligations and effective regulatory oversight. Moreover, mineral development must benefit local populations. Communities should receive their share of employment, as well as better public services and improved infrastructure. Without local support, even commercially viable projects can falter. Additionally, Islamabad must avoid becoming merely a supplier of raw materials to the world. Exporting unprocessed minerals will bring some foreign exchange, but it will not deliver wider economic gains. The real opportunity lies in transfer of technology for refining minerals and producing finished goods locally. This would require investment in processing facilities and related industries. The aim must be to build an industrial base around mineral resources rather than simply dig them out and ship them abroad. The state should also resist the temptation to present minerals as a solution to Pakistan’s long-term economic difficulties. They can contribute significantly to sustainable growth and help diversify exports. But no country has ever developed on mineral wealth or exports alone. Natural resources can provide capital for development, but they cannot replace the hard work of building productive industries. Mineral wealth must become part of a wider industrialisation strategy. The country needs to raise productivity across manufacturing and agriculture, and develop products that can find markets abroad.
articles.author: Editorial
